SECTION: 1. Attitudes toward algorithmic decision-making (Pages 9-21)

TOPICS: public attitudes, algorithmic bias, fairness, effectiveness, acceptability, survey methodology, demographic differences, specific applications (finance, hiring, criminal justice, social media), reasons for acceptance/rejection

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 58% of U.S. adults believe computer programs will always reflect human bias; 40% believe it is possible for them to be free from bias (Page 9)
- 50% of 18- to 29-year-olds believe bias-free programs are possible; 43% of 30- to 49-year-olds; 34% of 50+ year-olds (Page 9)
- The survey was conducted from May 29 to June 11, 2018 (Page 9)
- Survey asked about four real-life examples: automated personal finance score, criminal risk assessment, video job interview analysis, and computerized resume screening (Page 9)
- None of the four programs are viewed as fair by a clear majority of U.S. adults (Page 10)
- Only 32% find the "personal finance score" fair; 33% find the "video job interview analysis" fair (Page 10)
- 54% of Americans believe automated personal finance scores would be effective at identifying good customers; only 32% find it fair, creating a 22-percentage-point gap (Page 11)
- 61% of blacks believe a parole scoring algorithm would not be fair; 49% of whites; 38% of Hispanics (Page 11)
- 47% of Hispanics and 45% of blacks find the consumer finance score concept fair; 25% of whites (Page 11)
- 68% of Americans think using the personal finance score concept is unacceptable; 67% oppose computer-aided video analysis in hiring (Page 12)
- Among the 31% who find the automated personal finance score acceptable, 31% believe it would be effective at helping companies find good customers (Page 12)
- 68% of Americans think it is unacceptable for companies to use automated personal finance scores (Page 13)
- Among those who find it unacceptable, 26% cite privacy violations; 20% say it doesn't represent people accurately; 15% feel it's unfair or discriminatory (Page 13)
- 42% of Americans think the use of automated criminal risk score programs is acceptable (Page 14)
- 42% of U.S. adults say it is acceptable for the criminal justice system to use automated criminal risk scores; 56% do not (Page 15)
- Among those who find it acceptable, the top reason is that it "Would be effective" (16%); among those who find it not acceptable, the top reason is that "Every individual/circumstance is diff." (26%) (Page 15)
- 56% of Americans think this type of program [video analysis of job candidates] is not acceptable (Page 16)
- 26% believe every individual or circumstance is different and hard for a computer to capture; 25% argue the system precludes personal growth or has poor information; 12% worry about the lack of human involvement; 9% are concerned about unfair bias or profiling (Page 16)
- 32% of Americans think it is acceptable to use this tool when hiring (Page 16)
- 17% believe companies should have the right to hire however they see fit; 16% think it's acceptable because it's just one data point among many; 9% believe this analysis would be more objective than a traditional interview (Page 16)
- 32% of U.S. adults say automated job interview analysis is acceptable; 67% say it is not acceptable (Page 17)
- Among those who find it acceptable, 17% cite "Companies can hire however they want" as the main reason; among those who find it unacceptable, 20% cite "Would not work/is flawed" as the main reason (Page 17)
- A person might perform well in person but freeze during a camera interview (Page 18)
- Interviews should only be used for distant candidates to narrow down applicants, with final interviews requiring in-person interaction (Page 18)
- Computers cannot evaluate a person's personality or how they relate to others (Page 18)
- 41% of Americans think it is acceptable for companies to use automated resume screening (Page 19)
- 19% believe it saves time and money; 19% think it would be more accurate than manual screening; 16% feel companies can hire however they want (Page 19)
- 57% of U.S. adults find automated resume screening unacceptable (Page 19)
- Among those who find it unacceptable, 36% cite the removal of the human element as the primary reason (Page 19)
- 36% of respondents worry that automated hiring takes the human element out of the process; 23% feel the system is not fair or would not always get the best person for the job; 16% worry that people could game the system by using keywords to appeal to algorithms (Page 20)
- 74% of U.S. adults believe social media content does not accurately reflect how society feels about important issues; 25% disagree (Page 21)
- 37% of Black adults and 35% of Hispanic adults think social media paints an accurate portrait of society; 20% of white adults hold this view (Page 21)
- 35% of adults aged 18-29 think social media is accurate; 19% of those 65 and older (Page 21)

SECTION: 2. Algorithms in action: The content people see on social media (Pages 21-28)

TOPICS: public attitudes toward algorithms, emotional responses to content, content types and experiences, data privacy and acceptability, demographic differences, survey methodology

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- 74% of U.S. adults believe social media content does not accurately reflect how society feels about important issues; 25% disagree (Page 21)
- 37% of Black adults and 35% of Hispanic adults think social media provides an accurate picture of societal sentiment; 20% of white adults agree (Page 21)
- 35% of adults aged 18-29 believe social media reflects society accurately, compared to 19% of those 65+ (Page 21)
- 88% of social media users see content that makes them amused; 44% frequently experience this emotion (Page 22)
- 71% of users encounter content that makes them angry; 25% experience it frequently (Page 22)
- 71% see content that makes them feel connected, 69% feel inspired, 49% feel depressed, and 31% feel lonely (Page 22)
- 15% of users ages 18-29 frequently feel lonely, compared to 7% of ages 30-49 and 4% of those 50+ (Page 22)
- 30% of users aged 65+ frequently feel amused, while 24% frequently feel angry (Page 22)
- The "anger" emoticon is the most common reaction to congressional Facebook posts (Page 23)
- 31% of conservative Republicans and 27% of liberal Democrats frequently feel angry due to social media content (Page 23)
- 58% of users frequently see overly dramatic or exaggerated content (Page 23)
- 59% of users frequently see people making accusations or starting arguments without all facts (Page 23)
- 54% of social media users say they typically see an equal mix of kind/supportive and mean/bullying behavior; 21% see more kindness, 24% see more negativity (Page 24)
- 58% of users see overly dramatic or exaggerated posts frequently; 59% see people making accusations without all facts frequently (Page 24)

- Only 32% find the "personal finance score" fair; 33% find the "video job interview analysis" fair (Page 10)

- 61% of blacks believe a parole scoring algorithm would not be fair; 49% of whites; 38% of Hispanics (Page 11)
- 47% of Hispanics and 45% of blacks find the consumer finance score concept fair; 25% of whites (Page 11)
- 68% of Americans think using the personal finance score concept is unacceptable; 67% oppose computer-aided video analysis in hiring (Page 12)
- Among the 31% who find the automated personal finance score acceptable, 31% believe it would be effective at helping companies find good customers (Page 12)
- 68% of Americans think it is unacceptable for companies to use automated personal finance scores (Page 13)
- Among those who find it unacceptable, 26% cite privacy violations; 20% say it doesn't represent people accurately; 15% feel it's unfair or discriminatory (Page 13)
- 42% of Americans think the use of automated criminal risk score programs is acceptable (Page 14)
- 42% of U.S. adults say it is acceptable for the criminal justice system to use automated criminal risk scores; 56% do not (Page 15)
- Among those who find it acceptable, the top reason is that it "Would be effective" (16%); among those who find it not acceptable, the top reason is that "Every individual/circumstance is diff." (26%) (Page 15)
- 56% of Americans think this type of program [video analysis of job candidates] is not acceptable (Page 16)
- 26% believe every individual or circumstance is different and hard for a computer to capture; 25% argue the system precludes personal growth or has poor information; 12% worry about the lack of human involvement; 9% are concerned about unfair bias or profiling (Page 16)
- 32% of Americans think it is acceptable to use this tool when hiring (Page 16)
- 17% believe companies should have the right to hire however they see fit; 16% think it's acceptable because it's just one data point among many; 9% believe this analysis would be more objective than a traditional interview (Page 16)
- 32% of U.S. adults say automated job interview analysis is acceptable; 67% say it is not acceptable (Page 17)
- Among those who find it acceptable, 17% cite "Companies can hire however they want" as the main reason; among those who find it unacceptable, 20% cite "Would not work/is flawed" as the main reason (Page 17)
- A person might perform well in person but freeze during a camera interview (Page 18)
- Interviews should only be used for distant candidates to narrow down applicants, with final interviews requiring in-person interaction (Page 18)
- Computers cannot evaluate a person's personality or how they relate to others (Page 18)
- 41% of Americans think it is acceptable for companies to use automated resume screening (Page 19)
- 19% believe it saves time and money; 19% think it would be more accurate than manual screening; 16% feel companies can hire however they want (Page 19)
- 57% of U.S. adults find automated resume screening unacceptable (Page 19)
- Among those who find it unacceptable, 36% cite the removal of the human element as the primary reason (Page 19)
- 36% of respondents worry that automated hiring takes the human element out of the process; 23% feel the system is not fair or would not always get the best person for the job; 16% worry that people could game the system by using keywords to appeal to algorithms (Page 20)
- 74% of U.S. adults believe social media content does not accurately reflect how society feels about important issues; 25% disagree (Page 21)

Nearly all the content people see on social media is chosen not by human editors but rather by computer programs using massive quantities of data about each user to deliver content that he or she might find relevant or engaging. elements.text: The American Trends Panel Survey Methodology

The American Trends Panel (ATP), created by Pew Research Center, is a nationally representative panel of randomly selected U.S. adults recruited from landline and cellphone random-digit-dial (RDD) surveys. Panelists participate via monthly self-administered web surveys. Panelists who do not have internet access are provided with a tablet and wireless internet connection. The panel is being managed by GfK.

Data in this report are drawn from the panel wave conducted May 29-June 11, 2018, among 4,594 respondents. The margin of sampling error for the full sample of 4,594 respondents is plus or minus 2.4 percentage points.

Members of the American Trends Panel were recruited from several large, national landline and cellphone RDD surveys conducted in English and Spanish. At the end of each survey, respondents were invited to join the panel. The first group of panelists was recruited from the 2014 Political Polarization and Typology Survey, conducted Jan. 23 to March 16, 2014. Of the 10,013 adults interviewed, 9,809 were invited to take part in the panel and a total of 5,338 agreed to participate. $^{1}$  The second group of panelists was recruited from the 2015 Pew Research Center Survey on Government, conducted Aug. 27 to Oct. 4, 2015. Of the 6,004 adults interviewed, all were invited to join the panel, and 2,976 agreed to participate. $^{2}$  The third group of panelists was recruited from a survey conducted April 25 to June 4, 2017. Of the 5,012 adults interviewed in the survey or pretest, 3,905 were invited to take part in the panel and a total of 1,628 agreed to participate. $^{3}$

The ATP data were weighted in a multistep process that begins with a base weight incorporating the respondents' original survey selection probability and the fact that in 2014 some panelists were subsampled for invitation to the panel. Next, an adjustment was made for the fact that the propensity to join the panel and remain an active panelist varied across different groups in the sample. The final step in the weighting uses an iterative technique that aligns the sample to population benchmarks on a number of dimensions. Gender, age, education, race, Hispanic origin and region parameters come from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2016 American Community Survey.
